 NVDA Stock Rebounds Above $220 as Amazon Buys Billions in Nvidia Chips while Electricity Constraints Threaten Returns
 Nvidia shares have rebounded above $220 after falling from a record $243, but data-center power shortages, rising financing costs, semiconductor supply constraints and growing competition threaten the sustainability of the rally.
 Written by: 
 Skerdian Meta 
 • 
 Wednesday, October 21, 2026 
 • 
 4 min read 
 • 
 Last updated: Wednesday, October 21, 2026 
 Add an article to your Reading List Register now to be able to add articles to your reading list. SIGN UP Already have an account? Sign in " aria-hidden="true"> 
 Quick overview
 Nvidia shares have rebounded above $220 after a decline from a record $243, but face challenges from power shortages and rising costs.
 Amazon's power shortages have delayed the deployment of Nvidia hardware, raising concerns about immediate revenue generation.
 Expectations for higher memory prices support semiconductor sentiment, but increased costs may hinder infrastructure expansion.
 Nvidia's recovery is at risk due to competition from custom chips and uncertainty surrounding technology sector spending.
 Nvidia shares have rebounded above $220 after falling from a record $243, but data-center power shortages, rising financing costs, semiconductor supply constraints and growing competition threaten the sustainability of the rally. 
 Nvidia Stock Rebounds After Sharp Reversal
 Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shares recovered above $220 after retreating toward $212 last Friday, reversing part of their decline from a record above $243 earlier this month. The rebound reflects improving semiconductor sentiment, supported by expectations that memory shortages and higher prices could persist through 2027.
 However, the recovery comes amid growing concerns about the cost of expanding computing infrastructure. Investors are questioning whether technology companies can generate sufficient returns from their enormous investments, particularly as borrowing costs rise and competition intensifies.
 Although Nvidia remains a leading supplier of advanced processors, the latest developments highlight the financial and operational challenges facing its customers.
 Amazon’s Power Shortages Highlight Infrastructure Risks
 Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) is reportedly purchasing billions of dollars in Nvidia hardware, but some server racks are sitting in warehouses because data centers lack sufficient electricity to operate them, according to Business Insider.
 Internal emails reportedly indicated that Amazon expected to receive $5 billion in Nvidia server systems in August, followed by another $3 billion per month. The company also introduced an “Early Rack Receipt” program, allowing it to secure equipment before facilities are ready to use it.
 Previously, Amazon generally waited until hardware arrived at its data centers before taking ownership. The revised approach allows it to secure scarce equipment earlier, but also exposes the company to storage costs and delays between delivery and deployment.
 The situation illustrates a key risk for Nvidia: strong orders do not necessarily translate into immediate revenue generation for customers. If power shortages delay installations, returns on infrastructure investments could take longer to materialise, potentially affecting future spending decisions.
 Memory Prices Support Semiconductor Sentiment
 Expectations for higher memory prices have provided some support to semiconductor shares. Dell CEO Michael Dell reportedly warned that memory shortages could worsen in 2027, while analysts at Mizuho and KeyBanc have highlighted the potential for NAND flash prices to increase as infrastructure demand expands.
 Higher memory prices could benefit manufacturers across the supply chain, although they may also increase the cost of building and operating computing systems.
 For Nvidia, the key question is whether customers can continue expanding their infrastructure budgets while absorbing higher costs for memory, processors, electricity and data-center construction.
 NVIDIA Stock Reverses From the Highs
 NVIDIA shares lost momentum early in September after failing to break decisively above the $236 resistance zone, with the rejection sending the stock back below $210 but we have seen a decent rebound recently. Shares have climbed above $233 today as investors responded positively to expanding infrastructure partnerships and CEO projections, but buyers are not able to sustain the rally above $243 and we saw dive a below $213 again last week but we’re seeing some improvement this week.
 NVIDIA Stock Heads to MAs Again 
 ASML Warning Raises Supply Concerns
 ASML reported record third-quarter sales of €11.7 billion but warned that semiconductor manufacturing capacity planned for 2027 and 2028 might not fully satisfy expected demand.
 The company forecast fourth-quarter revenue of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion and narrowed its 2026 sales guidance to €44 billion–€45 billion. Despite these strong figures, its U.S.-listed shares reportedly fell around 4%, adding pressure to Nvidia and AMD.
 The warning highlights the difficulty of expanding production quickly enough to meet demand. Supply constraints could support semiconductor pricing, but they may also delay the delivery of equipment needed to sustain industry growth.
 CoreWeave Debt Signals Financing Pressure
 Financing concerns have intensified following heavy selling in CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV). Yields on its $1.25 billion bond issue due in 2032 reportedly reached 15% before closing around 14.5%, reflecting significant investor concern about credit risk.
 Such borrowing costs raise questions about the sustainability of debt-financed data-center expansion. If infrastructure operators face increasingly expensive financing, some projects could be delayed or scaled back, weakening future demand for Nvidia processors.
 Reports of potential large financing arrangements involving SpaceX and Nvidia GPUs, alongside Amazon’s exploration of chip-financing structures, further illustrate the capital required to maintain the expansion.
 Microsoft Custom Chips Challenge Nvidia
 Microsoft’s Maia 300 processor adds another competitive threat. The chip reportedly targets 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU systems, while a 96-accelerator configuration is designed to deliver up to seven times the rack-scale throughput of its predecessor.
 Custom silicon could help cloud providers improve efficiency and reduce dependence on external suppliers for selected workloads. Nvidia’s established ecosystem remains a major advantage, but increasing competition could eventually pressure its pricing power and market share in certain applications.
 OpenAI Revenue Questions Add Uncertainty
 Questions surrounding OpenAI’s revenue have also renewed scrutiny of technology-sector spending assumptions. Its annualised revenue run rate was reportedly around $50 billion at the end of September, below the widely circulated $68 billion figure, which reportedly included revenue generated by partners.
 Nvidia is also reportedly considering further investment in Reflection AI, although discussions have not resulted in a confirmed agreement. These developments highlight how investor sentiment increasingly depends on whether substantial infrastructure investments can be supported by sustainable commercial demand.
 Nvidia Stock Faces a Critical Test
 Nvidia’s rebound above $220 offers some relief after its retreat from $243, but the recovery remains vulnerable to renewed selling. Memory demand and continued semiconductor investment provide support, while power shortages, expensive financing and custom-chip competition complicate the outlook.
 A sustained recovery will require buyers to regain confidence that infrastructure spending can deliver sufficient returns. Until then, elevated valuations leave Nvidia exposed to further profit-taking if customers delay projects or expectations for future demand weaken.
